entities.name: African Orthodox Church
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The African Orthodox Church (AOC), founded in 1921 in New York by George Alexander McGuire — a Black Anglican priest from Antigua who had been associated with Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) — was one of the most significant African American religious institutions of the Harlem Renaissance era, representing the movement for Black religious self-determination that sought to liberate African American Christianity from white ecclesiastical control and create a church that honored the African heritage of its members.

George Alexander McGuire's founding of the African Orthodox Church reflected the broader Black nationalist intellectual movement of the 1920s: at a time when Marcus Garvey was promoting Pan-African pride through UNIA and the Black Star Line, McGuire created a church that deliberately broke with white-controlled denominations, established its own apostolic succession (through the Orthodox Christian succession line), and promoted a theology and liturgy that celebrated African identity — including controversially promoting representations of a Black Madonna and Black Christ as legitimate images.

The African Orthodox Church had an unexpected influence in East Africa: it provided apostolic succession to the Kikuyu-founded African Independent Pentecostal Church in Kenya and similar African Indigenous Christian movements that sought authentic Christian ordination independent of European missions. This African American-to-African ecclesiastical connection — flowing from Harlem's Black nationalism to East African independence-era Christianity — represents one of the most unusual trans-Atlantic religious connections of the 20th century.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The African Orthodox Church — founded during the Harlem Renaissance as a monument to Black religious self-determination, providing apostolic succession to East African independent churches — is historically significant as a Harlem Renaissance institution that connected Black American religious nationalism to African independent Christianity.
